questions.problem:
Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{121}$ be a random sample of size $n=121$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =300$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =55.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $295.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1587\,$ | $\,0.1562\,$ | $\,0.1539\,$ |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1841\,$ | $\,0.1814\,$ | $\,0.1788\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.2119\,$ | $\,0.2090\,$ | $\,0.2061\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=121,\,\mu =300,\,\sigma =55.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(300,\frac{{55}^{2}}{121}) \\  & ∼N(300,25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<295).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =P(Z<\frac{295-300}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z<-\frac{5}{5}) \\  & =P(Z<-1) \\  & =Φ(-1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1)=0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =Φ(-1) \\  & =0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}$ be a random sample of size $n=25$ from a population with probability density function 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}, & 0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15,$ calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$

*Hint: Assume that the sample size is sufficiently large for the central limit theorem to be applied. A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ | $\,0.8810\,$ | $\,0.8830\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{32}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2} \\  & =1.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.5,\frac{0.15}{25}) \\  & ∼N(1.5,0.006).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =P(Z>\frac{1.6-1.5}{\sqrt{0.006}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.29)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>1.29) & =1-P(Z<1.29) \\  & =1-Φ(1.29).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(1.29)=0.9015.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =1-Φ(1.29) \\  & =1-0.9015 \\  & =0.0985.\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{116}$ be a random sample of size $n=116$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $3$ and $5.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=116,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.6+5\cdot 0.1+10\cdot 0.2+15\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+0.5+2+1.5 \\  & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.6+{5}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{10}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{15}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{4}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.5+20+22.5)-16 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(4,\frac{29}{116}) \\  & ∼N(4,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5) & ≈P(\frac{3-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{5-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-2<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5)=Φ(2)-Φ(-2).
$$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=65,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.1+(-6)\cdot 0.4+(-4)\cdot 0.4+(-2)\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.8-2.4-1.6-0.2 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.1+(-6)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-5)^{2} \\  & =(6.4+14.4+6.4+0.4)-25 \\  & =2.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{2.6}{65}) \\  & ∼N(-5,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.9-(-5)}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.5) \\  & =Φ(0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9)=Φ(0.5).
$$
